questions.question: What is a network partition in distributed systems?

options.text: A failure where some nodes cannot communicate with others

questions.explanation: A network partition occurs when network failures prevent some nodes from communicating with others, splitting the cluster into isolated groups. Each group may continue operating independently, causing consistency issues.

questions.question: According to the CAP theorem, what must a system choose during a network partition?
questions.explanation: During a partition, a system must choose: remain consistent (reject requests that can't be verified across partitions) or remain available (serve requests with potentially stale/inconsistent data).

questions.question: A database cluster experiences a network partition. The minority partition has 2 of 5 nodes. What should happen in a CP system?

options.text: The minority partition stops accepting writes to maintain consistency
The minority partition becomes read-only automatically

questions.explanation: In CP systems, the minority partition cannot achieve quorum (3 of 5 needed). It must stop accepting writes to prevent split-brain inconsistency. The majority partition continues operating normally.

questions.question: What is a 'partial partition' in distributed systems?

options.text: A partition affecting only some data
When some nodes can communicate with some but not all other nodes
A partition in part of the network

questions.explanation: Partial partition: Node A can reach B, B can reach C, but A cannot reach C. More complex than full partition. Can cause subtle bugs where different nodes have different views of cluster membership.

questions.question: How do distributed systems typically detect network partitions?
questions.explanation: Nodes send periodic heartbeats. If heartbeats aren't received within timeout, the node is considered unreachable. Failure detectors (like Phi Accrual) provide probabilistic detection with tunable sensitivity.

questions.question: True or False: Network partitions are rare in modern cloud environments.
questions.explanation: Network partitions happen regularly in production: switch failures, cable issues, misconfiguration, cloud provider issues. Studies show partitions occur in all major cloud providers. Systems must be designed to handle them.

questions.question: What is 'partition tolerance' in the CAP theorem?

options.text: The system can be partitioned into smaller systems
The system continues operating despite network partitions

questions.explanation: Partition tolerance means the system continues to function when network partitions occur. In distributed systems, partitions are inevitable, so partition tolerance is effectively required—leaving the C vs A choice.

questions.question: A microservices system experiences a partition between Service A and Service B. What pattern helps Service A continue functioning?
questions.explanation: Circuit breaker detects failures and stops calling the unreachable service. Fallback provides degraded functionality (cached data, default response). This prevents cascade failures and maintains partial availability.

questions.question: What happens when a network partition heals?

options.text: Conflicting updates from both partitions must be reconciled

questions.explanation: If both partitions accepted writes (AP system), there may be conflicting updates. Reconciliation strategies: last-write-wins, merge (CRDTs), or manual conflict resolution. This is a key challenge in distributed systems.

questions.question: Which strategies help systems handle network partitions? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: Quorum ensures majority agreement (CP). Async replication with conflict resolution allows availability (AP). Graceful degradation maintains partial functionality. Single-node avoids distribution but isn't scalable/available.

questions.question: What is 'asymmetric partition'?

options.text: When A can send to B but B cannot send to A

questions.explanation: Asymmetric partition: one-way communication failure. A's messages reach B, but B's don't reach A. A thinks B is down; B thinks A is fine. This can cause subtle bugs in leader election and consensus.

questions.question: A distributed database uses synchronous replication. During a partition, what is the tradeoff?

options.text: No tradeoff, synchronous replication handles partitions
Writes block until partition heals, sacrificing availability for consistency

questions.explanation: Synchronous replication requires acknowledgment from replicas. During partition, writes to unreachable replicas block indefinitely or timeout. This maintains consistency but sacrifices availability—classic CP behavior.
